strengths: Clear problem identification: Demonstrates that coherency degradation in steering is undetectable by standard metrics (MMLU, PPL) and proposes a well-motivated solution

Rigorous experimental methodology with multiple analytical levels (layer-wise, head-wise, ablation studies), comprehensive metrics (trait, coherency, MMLU, PPL, IFEval), and strong human evaluation validation (92.8% agreement)
Technically sound geometric analysis approach using cosine similarity heatmaps and head contribution scores to efficiently identify persona-related components without prohibitive causal interventions

Consistent and clear empirical improvements: Head Cor steering achieves best Pareto frontiers in 11/12 conditions for Qwen2.5-7B and demonstrates superior trait-coherency trade-offs across all six personas

Excellent presentation with comprehensive visualizations, detailed appendices including qualitative examples, and novel Right-normalized Constrained Envelope Area metric for multi-objective evaluation
Practical significance for safer LLM deployment: Demonstrates functional modularity in transformers with implications for safer alignment and component-level control
weaknesses: Limited theoretical understanding: Paper identifies that 3 heads specialize in persona control but provides no mechanistic explanation for why or how this specialization emerges; the noise amplification hypothesis is intuitive but untested

Significant generalization concerns: Only two dense models tested (both GQA); Appendix F reveals Gemma3 shows fundamentally different behavior (multiple direction shifts vs. single transition); MoE results underdeveloped; different behavior for safety-related personas suggests post-training effects follow different mechanisms

Incomplete related work comparisons: No empirical evaluation against Angular Steering or Dynamic Steering despite mentioning these methods; only compares intervention points, not against alternative approaches to addressing coherency degradation

Architectural dependency limitations: Method requires per-model/per-architecture head identification; unclear if findings generalize beyond the tested models; Grouped Query Attention may be crucial for observed specialization

Mixed performance for safety-related traits: Section 5.3 shows Attn Residual outperforms Head Cor on MMLU/IFEval for safety personas, indicating harmful behaviors involve broader circuits beyond identified heads; limits utility for critical safety applications

Methodological concerns: Head identification threshold not formally defined; steering coefficient ranges differ between conditions (0.5-10.0 vs 0.5-14.0), confounding comparisons; human evaluation limited to 60 samples without significance testing; dot product metric (Eq. 4) loses directional information

Limited mechanistic insight: Lacks investigation of what these heads actually compute (attention patterns, feature properties); missing connections to sparsity and lottery ticket literature; no analysis of head attention patterns or learned representations

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing practical obstacle (coherency degradation in activation steering)
Comprehensive experimental validation: 6 personas, 2 primary models + 2 extended models, multiple metrics with human validation (91-92% agreement)
Elegant geometric analysis approach for localizing steering targets without exhaustive search
Strong and consistent empirical results with clear Pareto frontier improvements (Head Cor wins 11/12 conditions on Qwen2.5-7B)
Rigorous experimental design with appropriate ablations (causal verification, random controls, cross-run averaging)
Excellent reproducibility with 42-page appendices including prompts, protocols, and implementation details
Honest limitations discussion acknowledging architectural sensitivity and scope constraints
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: core insight (precise intervention reduces noise) is intuitive; execution is straightforward application of existing geometric analysis techniques

Serious generalizability concerns acknowledged in Section 7: Style Modulation Heads localization breaks down for larger models (Gemma-3-12B, Qwen3-30B) with multiple layers containing relevant heads and different architectural patterns; undermines broad claims about generality
Narrow application scope restricted to persona/style control; unclear if findings generalize to other steering targets (factual knowledge, reasoning, safety behaviors), limiting impact

Shallow mechanistic understanding: paper identifies 'where' to steer but not 'why' these heads are specialized or what information they process; no connection to known attention head functions (induction, copying)

Incomplete baseline comparisons: mainly compares intervention locations (residual stream variants) rather than alternative coherency-improvement methods (Angular Steering, Dynamic Steering, SAE-based approaches mentioned but not benchmarked)
Experimental bias: Head Cor tested with larger coefficient range (α ∈ [0.5, 14.0]) vs. others (α ∈ [0.5, 10.0]) with post-hoc justification; enables comparison bias

Missing failure mode analysis: underdeveloped discussion of when Head Cor underperforms (e.g., safety personas on Llama-3.1-8B for MMLU/IFEval); no characterization of persona properties enabling this approach
No statistical significance testing: 5 runs reported but no confidence intervals, standard deviations, or p-values; LLM-judge validation on small sample (10 pairs × 3 judges)
Persona vector quality dependency on contrastive prompts not analyzed for robustness; GPT-5 used to generate some prompts with minimal documentation
